notable_absence.finding: Four absences, and one of them is close to a documentation defect. (1) NO ACCESS CONTROL. A 15 KB page about a service that reads every bucket in the cluster and writes it to a filesystem or cloud location names no privilege, no role, and no credential requirement anywhere - and it links the Audit Event Reference, so the docs plainly know the service is security-relevant. (2) NO EDITION GATE. cbbackupmgr is documented in the tree as 'Enterprise Backup and Restore' (the seeAlso target is backup-restore/enterprise-backup-restore.md) yet this page never states that the Backup Service, or backup at all, requires Enterprise Edition. If it does, that fact is missing from the page a reader would consult; if it does not, the link title is misleading. Either way this is worth SME follow-up and I have asserted nothing about it. (3) NO dependsOnService. This is the only one of the four services in this batch that never states a dependency on the Data Service, even though it cannot back anything up without one. I looked for a sourceable sentence and there is none, so the relation is OMITTED rather than invented - saying so here as instructed, because the omission is the interesting part: the seventh service is architecturally disconnected from the service:* dependency graph purely because nobody wrote the sentence. (4) NO MEMORY QUOTA. Recorded above as a cross-page relation from services.md; absent from this page. Also absent and mildly surprising: no statement of a maximum or recommended number of Backup Service nodes, despite a whole section titled 'Choosing the Number of Backup Service Nodes' whose actual advice is 'one, unless you want resiliency'.

cross_component_finding: THREE IDS FOR ONE CLI TOOL. cbbackupmgr exists in the corpus as tool:cbbackupmgr (cloud/reference/command-line-tools.json), backup:cbbackupmgr (cloud/clusters/backup-restore.json, cli-backup-restore.json, manage-backup.json) and capella:cbbackupmgr (cloud/clusters/data-service/export.json). Five files, three namespaces, one utility, no registry entry. The registry already resolved exactly this shape once - tool:cbq-shell folding n1ql:cbq across 13 files, with the note 'n1ql: is for SQL++ language constructs; a CLI tool is not one' - so the precedent is clear and I have followed it by reusing tool:cbbackupmgr. Reconciliation should fold the other two. SECOND: 'Cluster Manager'. The registry holds capella:cluster-manager (component) and capella-role:cluster-manager (project role) and explicitly warns not to conflate them. This page now adds a third sighting - the Cluster Manager as the elector of the Backup Service leader on self-managed Couchbase - which I have had to record as server:cluster-manager because the existing component id is Capella-namespaced. That is two ids for one component, created purely by namespace convention, and it is a different kind of problem from the genuine role/component collision the registry already documents. THIRD, coordination models: backup:leader-node (cluster-wide singleton, externally elected, service stops without it) versus search:coordinator-node (per-request, self-assumed, no election). Two of four pages describe intra-service coordination and the two mechanisms are structurally unlike; kept as two concepts and two predicates (electsLeaderVia, assumedPerRequest) rather than one. FOURTH, a docs issue: the sentence 'You associate a plan with a repository where it stored backup data' is ungrammatical ('it stored' for 'it stores' or 'to store'), and the note in the Repositories section contains another - 'either one started directory or by the Backup Service' for 'started directly'. FIFTH, a structural observation relevant to the round's hypothesis: this page is filed under learn/ but behaves like reference material. It names literal setting identifiers (merge_offset_start, merge_offset_end, nodesThreadsMap), gives a formula for thread count, and works through numbered date examples. It produced 20 concepts and 34 relations against eventing-service.md's 5 and 6, from the same directory. The reference-versus-conceptual distinction this round set out to test does not track the docs' own directory structure.
cross_product_finding: THE BACKUP SERVICE HAS NO CAPELLA COUNTERPART, AND THIS IS THE SHARPEST DEPLOYMENT-MODEL DIVERGENCE IN THE BATCH. Grepping the whole cloud/ tree, the string 'Backup Service' occurs exactly once, in cloud/clusters/cloud-snapshots.md, and it does not refer to Couchbase at all: 'Your CSP's backup service, which is the underlying backup mechanism for your cluster backups, takes incremental storage snapshots for any backup after your first cluster backup.' In Capella the phrase means the cloud provider's snapshot facility. So the same two words denote a deployable Couchbase service in server/ and a third-party AWS/GCP/Azure mechanism in cloud/ - a cross-product name collision of the same class as the registry's existing cluster-manager and four-way role writeups, but this one spans products rather than living inside one. Beyond the name: round 6-9's Capella backup extraction produced a completely different ontology for the same user need - backup:bucket-backup vs backup:cluster-backup (Cloud Snapshot), backup:backup-cycle, backup:cost-optimized-retention-policy, backup:downloadable-backup, cloud-provider:* variation, gatedByBillingPlan, and capella-role:* gating on every procedural page. NONE of those appear here, and none of this page's vocabulary - plan, repository, leader election, task overlap, thread count, merge offsets, archived repositories - appears there. The two trees share only backup:full-backup and backup:incremental-backup. Note the inversion of the pattern seen elsewhere in this batch: for Search and Analytics, Capella supplied the semantics and server/ supplied the infrastructure; for Backup, server/ supplies BOTH, and Capella replaces the service with a managed feature plus a billing model. The practical consequence for the ontology: service:backup-service is a concept that can only ever have self-managed instances, and any query of the form 'which services does Couchbase have' returns six or seven depending silently on which tree was ingested.
